input.rationale: CheckRun 69ae511befca4c7ea390e6b944da8179 returned completed/tests_passed with exit 0, 17 parsed CA_EVENT observations and 0 parsing errors. Indices 0-15 reproduce the three earlier probes with identical operands, and index 16 is the only output of the new sweep case: invariant_sweep_summary with seeds=60, steps_per_seed=60, elections=459, proposals=446 and violations=0. That summary is the receipt for the invariant-sweep question, so I interpret it here as a holds-only result over a fixed event set, record explicitly that the executed event set is narrower than the registered discriminator (the sweep that ran contains no ConfChange proposals, no joint configuration and no node restart, even though the discriminator named them), and register that shortfall as a necessary gap on this investigation rather than letting the summary stand as if it covered them. No new experiment is requested this turn: the next case must add configuration changes and restarts to the same sweep, which is construction work.

gaps.question: The executed sweep covered elections, proposals, ticks, isolate/recover, TransferLeader and persist/apply cycles, but not the configuration changes (simple and joint) and node restarts that the registered discriminator named. Do the four checked invariants still hold once ConfChangeV2 proposals (including joint transitions and learner promotions) and restarts of a node from its persisted MemoryStorage are included in the randomized event set, and does the campaign guard's applied-lag condition ever leave a live cluster without an electable voter in that wider set?

interpretations.rationale: Index 16 reports the sweep's only output: 60 seeds times 60 steps produced 459 elections and 446 proposals with violations=0, and the event carries the note that absence of violations is a holds-only result for this event set rather than a safety proof. For the four invariants actually checked after every event - at most one leader per term, no index already known committed ever observed with a different term, per-node committed-index monotonicity, and applied <= committed - the receipt therefore contains no counterexample, which is consistent with the source-level explanation that commitment and leadership require quorum-intersecting support under the simple configuration used here (MajorityConfig.CommittedIndex/VoteResult with the joint min/majority semantics). The absence is nevertheless bounded by what the harness actually did: it emitted no violation event of any of the four kinds, and it also emitted no configuration-change or restart event, because the executed case omits both while the registered discriminator named them. I am recording that as a necessary gap and keeping the conclusion scoped to the exercised event set; the defect claim is refuted only in the narrow sense that this event set produced no witness for the suspicion, not because the invariants were established for the protocol.
counterevidence: The sweep's coverage is smaller than the discriminator promised: no ConfChange/ConfChangeV2 proposal, no joint or learner configuration and no restart from persisted storage appeared in the event stream, so the mechanism most likely to threaten the invariants (support counted under a configuration that changes while entries are unapplied) was not part of this receipt.

A zero-violation count over 60 seeds cannot bound the violation rate; it states only that no witness appeared in this fixed event set, and the harness checked committed terms only for indices the nodes actually reported as committed, so an entry committed by a majority but never observed at any checked node is invisible to it.
limitations: Invariant checking happens after each event, not during message delivery, so an intermediate inconsistency that is repaired before the next check point would not be observed.
The committed-entry check compares terms at an index rather than full entry identity, which is adequate for log-matching violations but does not by itself detect a same-term payload difference.
Application is modelled with nextEnts on every step, so the applied index is never more than one event behind committed; a real application's lag patterns are not represented.
No comparison or requirement anchors were declared for this case in the experiment request, so the receipt carries parsed events only and its meaning rests on this interpretation.

investigations.question: In this snapshot, ReadOnlySafe confirmation is count-based rather than commit-index-based (read_only.go addRequest/recvAck/maybeAdvance/heartbeatCtx with confirmedReads, driven from stepLeader MsgHeartbeatResp and sendMsgReadIndexResponse). Which conditions establish that a released ReadState carries an index at least as new as the commit index at the moment the request was admitted, and what happens to still-unconfirmed reads when the leader's term changes (reset() rebuilds readOnly) or when the leader is a fresh leader that has not yet committed an entry in its term (pendingReadIndexMessages)?
investigations.hypothesis: A released read index is never smaller than the commit index recorded at admission of that read request, because positions are monotonic counts and acks are per-voter maxima; the open risk is a lost completion (request dropped by reset/term change) rather than a stale index.
investigations.discriminator: Drive a real 3-node cluster in one process: elect a leader, admit a read request (MsgReadIndex via Step), delay only MsgHeartbeatResp so no quorum ack exists yet, then remove the leader (isolate) and elect a new leader that commits an entry. Deliver the delayed heartbeat responses to the stale leader and record every ReadState and every dropped request. Expected if the count-based claim holds: no ReadState is emitted whose Index is below the commit index at admission; expected counter-shape: an emitted ReadState with a too-small Index (stale read) or a request that is silently never answered after the leader's term changed (lost completion).

gaps.question: Is an unconfirmed ReadIndex request answered, dropped, or answered with a stale index when the leader loses its term between admission and quorum acknowledgement, and which of those outcomes is observable from the ReadState stream?

investigations.question: hup() refuses to campaign whenever hasUnappliedConfChanges() is true, i.e. whenever any entry in (applied, committed] is an EntryConfChange/EntryConfChangeV2, and promotable() additionally vetoes campaign while an unstable or in-progress snapshot exists. No existing test references hasUnappliedConfChanges directly. Which permitted histories leave a node with committed-but-unapplied configuration entries, and can such a node campaign with a voter set that does not include its own committed configuration (for example after restoring a snapshot, after ReadIndex-style lag in application, or when the application rejects a config change by zeroing NodeId)?
investigations.hypothesis: The guard is a deliberate safety measure (campaign only with an applied configuration) and is correct for the paths it covers, but its interaction with (a) applied<committed gaps created by the application, (b) MsgTimeoutNow-triggered campaigning, and (c) restore/bootstrap paths is untested and may either block a legal transfer or admit a campaign with a stale voter set.
investigations.discriminator: Construct a voter whose storage holds a committed EntryConfChangeV2 that the application has not applied (Config.Applied below committed) and whose stored ConfState predates it, then (i) tick into an election timeout and (ii) deliver MsgTimeoutNow, and read back whether it becomes candidate, which voter IDs it addresses in the MsgVote/MsgPreVote messages, and which quorum quorum.VoteResult uses; the alternative outcome to distinguish is a campaign that proceeds despite the unapplied change, or a permanent inability to campaign after the application refuses the change.

gaps.question: With a committed-but-unapplied conf change in the log, does the node refrain from campaigning (and if so, is a later campaign possible once application catches up), and which voter set would a campaign use if it did proceed?

investigations.question: The campaign guard is verified to suppress a MsgTimeoutNow-triggered campaign when the transferee has a committed-but-unapplied conf change (CheckRun 238d3a23d8624c438b85ec18f90a7b2b events 0-2). Which observable sequence follows for a requested leadership transfer whose transferee lags application: does the leader keep sending MsgTimeoutNow/MsgApp until tickHeartbeat aborts the transfer at the election timeout, can the cluster still make progress through the existing leader in the meantime (proposals dropped while leadTransferee != None), and is a later transfer possible once the transferee's application catches up? This is the bounded-liveness side of the same guard, where a duty the leader explicitly accepted (transfer) cannot complete and the leader also refuses proposals.
investigations.hypothesis: The transfer neither completes nor deadlocks: the transferee refuses to campaign while the conf change is unapplied, the leader keeps proposing the transfer (and drops new proposals) until its election timeout elapses, then abortLeaderTransfer() clears leadTransferee and proposals resume, so the cost is bounded by one election timeout and the transfer can be retried after the transformer catches up.
investigations.discriminator: In one process, elect a 3-node leader, give the transferee a committed-but-unapplied conf-change entry (applied < committed) via its storage/HardState and Config.Applied, call TransferLeader to it, then tick the leader past its election timeout and record: whether MsgTimeoutNow was sent, whether MsgProp is rejected with ErrProposalDropped while leadTransferee != None, whether leadTransferee is cleared after the timeout, and whether a second TransferLeader attempt after applying the entry completes with the transferee campaigning at term+1. Expected if the claim holds: transfer aborted within one election timeout, proposals accepted again afterwards, second attempt succeeding after application catches up; the alternative to distinguish is a forever-pending transfer (leadTransferee never cleared or proposals permanently dropped) or a transfer that completes with a stale voter set.

investigations.question: The two answered questions and the transfer probe all exercise single, hand-built prefixes: one conf-change entry with applied lag, one read admission followed by one term change, one requested transfer. Which safety relationships survive a randomized sequence of permitted events produced by the snapshot's own producers - elections, proposals, configuration changes (simple and joint), partitions and recovery, compaction and leadership transfer - under the invariants the implementation itself relies on: at most one leader per term, no two nodes ever committing different entries at the same index, no node's committed index regressing, applied never exceeding committed, and every committed entry staying committed after a leader change? The aim is to look for a source-grounded counterexample to a safety property rather than to confirm the documented conservative behaviors already established.
investigations.hypothesis: No counterexample exists among these invariants for the exercised event set, because the decisions that justify commitment and leadership are quorum-intersecting under both simple and joint configurations, and the probes already show the campaign and read paths being conservative rather than permissive; a counterexample, if the sweep finds one, would have to come from a path where a decision is taken under a configuration that does not intersect the configuration used to commit the entries it relies on.
investigations.discriminator: Randomized in-process sweep over the repository's own network and storage helpers with a fixed seed set: each iteration builds a fresh 3-5 node cluster, applies a random sequence of permitted events (MsgHup on a random node, proposals of distinct payloads, simple and joint ConfChange proposals, isolate/recover of random nodes, tick bursts, TransferLeader to a random voter, compaction of a random node's applied prefix, and restart of a random node from its persisted storage), and after every event checks at most-one-leader-per-term, divergence of (index, term, payload) among all applied entries, monotonicity of each node's committed index, applied <= committed, and that no previously committed entry is ever overwritten. A single violation witness (seed, event number, node ids, the two conflicting (index, term) operands) is the discriminator; sustained absence over the seed set leaves the invariants holds-only for this event set and must not be reported as a safety proof.

interpretations.rationale: Source-only reading of the count-based read-only flow. Positive part: positions are monotonically increasing counts (never reused for a later batch), acks are maxima, and a released read carries the commit index recorded at admission, so a confirmed read cannot be justified by acknowledgements collected for an earlier request; the leader's own ack is the admission position, so a majority echo is still required for confirmation, and pendingReadIndexMessages are answered only after the leader commits in its term, which can only raise the emitted index. Unresolved part: the term-change path. reset() replaces r.readOnly with a fresh instance (unconfirmed reads and acks dropped) while r.readStates is untouched, and releasePendingReadIndexMessages only replies when committedEntryInCurrentTerm() holds. I have not yet observed whether a read admitted just before a term change is dropped silently (a lost completion under a legal trigger) or answered later; the snapshot's own TestReadOnlyDuplicateRequest covers only the duplicate-ctx/delayed-heartbeat case and asserts indices are not too small, not that every admitted request completes.
counterevidence: The repo's own read-index selections (TestReadOnlyOptionSafe/Lease/WithLearner/ForNewLeader/DuplicateRequest, TestRaftFreesReadOnlyMem) pass in native local feedback, and TestReadOnlyDuplicateRequest explicitly asserts no too-small read index under delayed duplicate requests plus a leader change, which weakens the stale-index side of the suspicion.
limitations: No retained execution receipt yet: the local test runs are construction feedback and cannot establish a formal conclusion.

Doc.go's Ready/Advance contract does not state that every admitted ReadIndex request must be answered, so a dropped request would have to be argued as a bounded-liveness consequence of an actual trigger rather than a contract violation.

interpretations.rationale: Source-only reading of the campaign admission guard. hasUnappliedConfChanges scans (applied, committed] with pagination and returns true on the first conf-change entry; hup() then refuses to campaign, and promotable() independently refuses while a snapshot is pending/unstable. The guard is consistent with doc.go's statement that configurations take effect when applied, and with applyConfChange/switchToConfig which only reconfigure on application, so a node that campaigns while lagging application would otherwise campaign with a stale voter set. What remains open is whether the guard is complete for the paths that can present a stale voter set (restore from snapshot with only ConfState initialized, bootstrap with applied<committed, an application that rejects a change by zeroing NodeId, and MsgTimeoutNow where the guard also suppresses a requested transfer), and whether the suppression can be permanent for an otherwise eligible voter.
limitations: No existing test references hasUnappliedConfChanges directly, so its behavior is currently only read from source; it must be probed with a real log/apply prefix rather than asserted.

interpretations.rationale: The suspicion had two branches: (i) the guard may be bypassed so a node campaigns with a stale voter set, and (ii) the guard may permanently block a legal campaign. Branch (i) is refuted by events 1 and 2: with has_unapplied=true and an already-promotable voter, both the MsgHup path and the MsgTimeoutNow path leave the node in StateFollower(term=1) with msgs=0, and the runner log shows the same suppression reason on both paths, so the transfer path reaches campaign() only through the same guard. The voter set used when campaigning is legitimate rather than stale: after the application catches up (event 3) the node reports has_unapplied=false and campaigns at term 2 with vote=1 and MsgVote addressed to voters [2,3], and event 0 records that this config (voters_before=[1,2,3]) is the applied configuration. Branch (ii) is refuted by the same event 3 plus the control at events 4-5: the block is transient, keyed on the entry type in (applied, committed] rather than on the applied/committed gap itself (the control has the identical gap and campaigns immediately). What remains is a bounded-liveness cost, not a safety defect: while the entry is unapplied the node cannot campaign and cannot take over a requested transfer, which is the documented intent that configurations take effect on application.

c6f44be10c0445b7a091b7db545cd614-gap-1.explanation: With a committed-but-unapplied conf change the node refrains from campaigning on both triggers (events 1-2: StateFollower, term 1, msgs=0; runner log 'cannot campaign at term 1 since there are still pending configuration changes to apply' on the MsgHup and MsgTimeoutNow paths), and a later campaign is possible once raft's applied index covers the entry (event 3: has_unapplied=false, StateCandidate at term 2, MsgVote to voters [2,3]; control events 4-5 show the effect is caused by the entry type, not by the applied/committed gap).

knowledge.assertion: hup() returns without campaigning when hasUnappliedConfChanges() is true, for both MsgHup and MsgTimeoutNow
campaign() addresses vote requests to the tracked voters of the current configuration, here [2,3]

counterevidence: The node is promotable=true throughout (events 0, 4), so the refusal does not come from promotable(); it is specifically hasUnappliedConfChanges, which strengthens the reading that the guard is the cause rather than an admission in promotable.

The post-apply campaign (event 3) carries vote targets [2,3] from the pre-change configuration because the harness only advanced raftLog.applied without calling ApplyConfChange; the voter set used in the probe is therefore the stored config, which is the config a leader would legitimately campaign with at that point.
limitations: The probe drives MsgHup/MsgTimeoutNow directly on a node whose storage prefix and Config.Applied are supplied, not a tick-driven election of a live cluster, so it establishes the guard's effect and its transience but not the wall-clock or tick cost of the suppression inside a running cluster.

The bounded-liveness cost for a requested transfer (leader keeps dropping proposals while leadTransferee != None) is visible in source but was not exercised by this harness; it is registered as investigation @transfer_stall.

interpretations.rationale: The question had two possible defect shapes: a stale (too small) read index, or a lost completion. Events 6-9 select the second and exclude the first for the exercised path. Event 7 shows the request admitted with unconfirmed_reads=1, read_states=0 and the admission commit index recorded as 2; event 8 shows that after the term change the node holds read_states=0, unconfirmed_reads=0, confirmed_reads=0 and ctx_A_completed=false, so the request is dropped, never emitted with a smaller index. Event 9 is the control that separates 'drops on term change' from 'read confirmation is broken': a read admitted on the new leader (commit_now=3, index_B=3) goes from read_states_before_ack=0 to read_states_after_ack=1 with ctx_B_completed=true as soon as one peer heartbeat response carrying the leader's context arrives, which is also the count-based confirmation the source predicted. A dropped completion is not a defect under the applicable contract: Node.ReadIndex documents that the request can be lost without notice and that ensuring read index retries is the user's job, so the caller duty is established by the target's own interface statement, and the exercised drop is exactly that documented lossiness rather than a wrong index being served.

c6f44be10c0445b7a091b7db545cd614-gap-0.explanation: The request is dropped, not answered stale: after admission with unconfirmed_reads=1 (event 7), the term change leaves read_states=0, unconfirmed_reads=0, confirmed_reads=0 and ctx_A_completed=false (event 8), so nothing is emitted for that context and no smaller index can be observed; the confirmation path itself still functions on the new leader (event 9: ctx_B_completed=true with index_B=3 equal to the commit index at admission), and the lossiness is the caller duty stated by Node.ReadIndex.

knowledge.assertion: a released ReadState is justified by a quorum of ack positions and carries the commit index recorded at admission

limitations: The probe steps MsgReadIndex directly into the leader rather than through Node.ReadIndex/RawNode.ReadIndex, so it shows the state-machine outcome and not the API-level return value or the Ready/ReadStates plumbing; the documented caller duty was read from node.go/doc.go rather than exercised.

Only one trigger of the term change was exercised (a higher-term campaign message from a peer); other authority losses that rebuild readOnly (for example a snapshot restore or a leadership transfer racing an admitted read) were not covered.
interpretations.joint_history: Same single invocation as the campaign-admission interpretation: CheckRun 238d3a23d8624c438b85ec18f90a7b2b is one execution of one fixed harness (fixed-experiments/075c21493fd94adc9bdc30a30b2cbff1-experiment/assurance_generated_test.go) containing both probes, so events 6-9 and events 0-5 come from the same process, the same fixed inputs and the same receipt, with no separate producer or intermediate history between them. The experiment record is attached to question-1 because the submission can carry only one experiment request; the receipt itself is shared, and its parsed indices 6-9 are the decisive operands for this question.

interpretations.rationale: The declared hypothesis was that the transfer neither completes nor deadlocks but is bounded by one election timeout, with proposals resuming afterwards and the transfer becoming possible once the transferee applies its committed configuration. The receipt confirms each leg in order. Event 10 establishes the prefix the claim needs: the leader is StateLeader(term 1, committed 2), the transferee is StateFollower with applied 0 and committed 2 and has_unapplied true, and the leader already has the transferee matched to its last index (r1_match_r2 2 == r1_last_index 2), which is exactly the condition under which the leader sends MsgTimeoutNow immediately. Event 11 shows the transfer is accepted as a pending duty (lead_transferee 2) while the transferee does not campaign (StateFollower, term 1), so the guard is what stops the handover rather than a transport or match problem. Event 12 shows the cost is real but scoped: a proposal during the window returns 'raft proposal dropped' (is_proposal_dropped true). Event 13 shows the bound: after the leader's electionTimeout ticks, lead_transferee is 0, the leader is still StateLeader(term 1) and a proposal is accepted again (proposal_err empty), i.e. abortLeaderTransfer released the pending duty within one election timeout instead of leaving it forever pending. Events 14-15 show the duty is transferable rather than lost: once the transferee's applied index reaches its committed index (has_unapplied false), the retried transfer completes with the transferee as StateLeader(term 2) and the former leader as StateFollower(term 2). A delayed transfer whose delay is caused by the transferee's own application lag, with the old leader still able to serve proposals after the abort, is not a defect under the stated conditions; the honest counterweight is that during the window the leader rejects client proposals, which is a client-visible cost of a request the application itself asked for, and the sweep of random configurations and authority changes remains to be done.

knowledge.assertion: hup() refuses to campaign on the leadership-transfer path reached via MsgTimeoutNow while hasUnappliedConfChanges() is true
campaign() addresses vote requests only to the tracked voters of the current configuration, as in the completed retry at term 2

counterevidence: Event 12 shows a proposal is rejected with ErrProposalDropped while the transfer is pending, so the bounded-liveness account must not be read as 'no cost': the cost is a proposal-rejection window whose length is determined by the transferee's application lag, and the receipt only measures it for one tick-driven abort (event 13) rather than for a live cluster's scheduling.

Events 10-15 exercise one configuration (three voters plus a staged learner) and one transfer target; nothing in the receipt constrains the same sequence during a joint configuration or when the transferee is the only node lagging while the rest are applied.
limitations: Application lag is modelled by not advancing raftLog.applied on the transferee; the receipt therefore shows the protocol's behavior given that lag, not how a real application creates it.
The abort was produced by ticking the leader through its own electionTimeout, so the bound observed is in protocol ticks under this harness's scheduling rather than wall-clock time.

The transfer completes in the receipt through the network's MsgTimeoutNow delivery on the retry; no independent completion path (for example a transfer while the leader is also being removed) was exercised.

Unresolved part: the term-change path. reset() replaces r.readOnly with a fresh instance (unconfirmed reads and acks dropped) while r.readStates is untouched, and releasePendingReadIndexMessages only replies when committedEntryInCurrentTerm() holds. I have not yet observed whether a read admitted just before a term change is dropped silently (a lost completion under a legal trigger) or answered later; the snapshot's own TestReadOnlyDuplicateRequest covers only the duplicate-ctx/delayed-heartbeat case and asserts indices are not too small, not that every admitted request completes.
counterevidence: The repo's own read-index selections (TestReadOnlyOptionSafe/Lease/WithLearner/ForNewLeader/DuplicateRequest, TestRaftFreesReadOnlyMem) pass in native local feedback, and TestReadOnlyDuplicateRequest explicitly asserts no too-small read index under delayed duplicate requests plus a leader change, which weakens the stale-index side of the suspicion.
limitations: No retained execution receipt yet: the local test runs are construction feedback and cannot establish a formal conclusion.

Doc.go's Ready/Advance contract does not state that every admitted ReadIndex request must be answered, so a dropped request would have to be argued as a bounded-liveness consequence of an actual trigger rather than a contract violation.

interpretations.rationale: Source-only reading of the campaign admission guard. hasUnappliedConfChanges scans (applied, committed] with pagination and returns true on the first conf-change entry; hup() then refuses to campaign, and promotable() independently refuses while a snapshot is pending/unstable. The guard is consistent with doc.go's statement that configurations take effect when applied, and with applyConfChange/switchToConfig which only reconfigure on application, so a node that campaigns while lagging application would otherwise campaign with a stale voter set. What remains open is whether the guard is complete for the paths that can present a stale voter set (restore from snapshot with only ConfState initialized, bootstrap with applied<committed, an application that rejects a change by zeroing NodeId, and MsgTimeoutNow where the guard also suppresses a requested transfer), and whether the suppression can be permanent for an otherwise eligible voter.
limitations: No existing test references hasUnappliedConfChanges directly, so its behavior is currently only read from source; it must be probed with a real log/apply prefix rather than asserted.

interpretations.rationale: The suspicion had two branches: (i) the guard may be bypassed so a node campaigns with a stale voter set, and (ii) the guard may permanently block a legal campaign. Branch (i) is refuted by events 1 and 2: with has_unapplied=true and an already-promotable voter, both the MsgHup path and the MsgTimeoutNow path leave the node in StateFollower(term=1) with msgs=0, and the runner log shows the same suppression reason on both paths, so the transfer path reaches campaign() only through the same guard. The voter set used when campaigning is legitimate rather than stale: after the application catches up (event 3) the node reports has_unapplied=false and campaigns at term 2 with vote=1 and MsgVote addressed to voters [2,3], and event 0 records that this config (voters_before=[1,2,3]) is the applied configuration. Branch (ii) is refuted by the same event 3 plus the control at events 4-5: the block is transient, keyed on the entry type in (applied, committed] rather than on the applied/committed gap itself (the control has the identical gap and campaigns immediately). What remains is a bounded-liveness cost, not a safety defect: while the entry is unapplied the node cannot campaign and cannot take over a requested transfer, which is the documented intent that configurations take effect on application.

c6f44be10c0445b7a091b7db545cd614-gap-1.explanation: With a committed-but-unapplied conf change the node refrains from campaigning on both triggers (events 1-2: StateFollower, term 1, msgs=0; runner log 'cannot campaign at term 1 since there are still pending configuration changes to apply' on the MsgHup and MsgTimeoutNow paths), and a later campaign is possible once raft's applied index covers the entry (event 3: has_unapplied=false, StateCandidate at term 2, MsgVote to voters [2,3]; control events 4-5 show the effect is caused by the entry type, not by the applied/committed gap).

knowledge.assertion: hup() returns without campaigning when hasUnappliedConfChanges() is true, for both MsgHup and MsgTimeoutNow
campaign() addresses vote requests to the tracked voters of the current configuration, here [2,3]

counterevidence: The node is promotable=true throughout (events 0, 4), so the refusal does not come from promotable(); it is specifically hasUnappliedConfChanges, which strengthens the reading that the guard is the cause rather than an admission in promotable.

The post-apply campaign (event 3) carries vote targets [2,3] from the pre-change configuration because the harness only advanced raftLog.applied without calling ApplyConfChange; the voter set used in the probe is therefore the stored config, which is the config a leader would legitimately campaign with at that point.
limitations: The probe drives MsgHup/MsgTimeoutNow directly on a node whose storage prefix and Config.Applied are supplied, not a tick-driven election of a live cluster, so it establishes the guard's effect and its transience but not the wall-clock or tick cost of the suppression inside a running cluster.

The bounded-liveness cost for a requested transfer (leader keeps dropping proposals while leadTransferee != None) is visible in source but was not exercised by this harness; it is registered as investigation @transfer_stall.

interpretations.rationale: The question had two possible defect shapes: a stale (too small) read index, or a lost completion. Events 6-9 select the second and exclude the first for the exercised path. Event 7 shows the request admitted with unconfirmed_reads=1, read_states=0 and the admission commit index recorded as 2; event 8 shows that after the term change the node holds read_states=0, unconfirmed_reads=0, confirmed_reads=0 and ctx_A_completed=false, so the request is dropped, never emitted with a smaller index. Event 9 is the control that separates 'drops on term change' from 'read confirmation is broken': a read admitted on the new leader (commit_now=3, index_B=3) goes from read_states_before_ack=0 to read_states_after_ack=1 with ctx_B_completed=true as soon as one peer heartbeat response carrying the leader's context arrives, which is also the count-based confirmation the source predicted. A dropped completion is not a defect under the applicable contract: Node.ReadIndex documents that the request can be lost without notice and that ensuring read index retries is the user's job, so the caller duty is established by the target's own interface statement, and the exercised drop is exactly that documented lossiness rather than a wrong index being served.

c6f44be10c0445b7a091b7db545cd614-gap-0.explanation: The request is dropped, not answered stale: after admission with unconfirmed_reads=1 (event 7), the term change leaves read_states=0, unconfirmed_reads=0, confirmed_reads=0 and ctx_A_completed=false (event 8), so nothing is emitted for that context and no smaller index can be observed; the confirmation path itself still functions on the new leader (event 9: ctx_B_completed=true with index_B=3 equal to the commit index at admission), and the lossiness is the caller duty stated by Node.ReadIndex.

knowledge.assertion: a released ReadState is justified by a quorum of ack positions and carries the commit index recorded at admission

limitations: The probe steps MsgReadIndex directly into the leader rather than through Node.ReadIndex/RawNode.ReadIndex, so it shows the state-machine outcome and not the API-level return value or the Ready/ReadStates plumbing; the documented caller duty was read from node.go/doc.go rather than exercised.

Only one trigger of the term change was exercised (a higher-term campaign message from a peer); other authority losses that rebuild readOnly (for example a snapshot restore or a leadership transfer racing an admitted read) were not covered.
interpretations.joint_history: Same single invocation as the campaign-admission interpretation: CheckRun 238d3a23d8624c438b85ec18f90a7b2b is one execution of one fixed harness (fixed-experiments/075c21493fd94adc9bdc30a30b2cbff1-experiment/assurance_generated_test.go) containing both probes, so events 6-9 and events 0-5 come from the same process, the same fixed inputs and the same receipt, with no separate producer or intermediate history between them. The experiment record is attached to question-1 because the submission can carry only one experiment request; the receipt itself is shared, and its parsed indices 6-9 are the decisive operands for this question.

interpretations.rationale: The declared hypothesis was that the transfer neither completes nor deadlocks but is bounded by one election timeout, with proposals resuming afterwards and the transfer becoming possible once the transferee applies its committed configuration. The receipt confirms each leg in order. Event 10 establishes the prefix the claim needs: the leader is StateLeader(term 1, committed 2), the transferee is StateFollower with applied 0 and committed 2 and has_unapplied true, and the leader already has the transferee matched to its last index (r1_match_r2 2 == r1_last_index 2), which is exactly the condition under which the leader sends MsgTimeoutNow immediately. Event 11 shows the transfer is accepted as a pending duty (lead_transferee 2) while the transferee does not campaign (StateFollower, term 1), so the guard is what stops the handover rather than a transport or match problem. Event 12 shows the cost is real but scoped: a proposal during the window returns 'raft proposal dropped' (is_proposal_dropped true). Event 13 shows the bound: after the leader's electionTimeout ticks, lead_transferee is 0, the leader is still StateLeader(term 1) and a proposal is accepted again (proposal_err empty), i.e. abortLeaderTransfer released the pending duty within one election timeout instead of leaving it forever pending. Events 14-15 show the duty is transferable rather than lost: once the transferee's applied index reaches its committed index (has_unapplied false), the retried transfer completes with the transferee as StateLeader(term 2) and the former leader as StateFollower(term 2). A delayed transfer whose delay is caused by the transferee's own application lag, with the old leader still able to serve proposals after the abort, is not a defect under the stated conditions; the honest counterweight is that during the window the leader rejects client proposals, which is a client-visible cost of a request the application itself asked for, and the sweep of random configurations and authority changes remains to be done.

knowledge.assertion: hup() refuses to campaign on the leadership-transfer path reached via MsgTimeoutNow while hasUnappliedConfChanges() is true
campaign() addresses vote requests only to the tracked voters of the current configuration, as in the completed retry at term 2

counterevidence: Event 12 shows a proposal is rejected with ErrProposalDropped while the transfer is pending, so the bounded-liveness account must not be read as 'no cost': the cost is a proposal-rejection window whose length is determined by the transferee's application lag, and the receipt only measures it for one tick-driven abort (event 13) rather than for a live cluster's scheduling.

Events 10-15 exercise one configuration (three voters plus a staged learner) and one transfer target; nothing in the receipt constrains the same sequence during a joint configuration or when the transferee is the only node lagging while the rest are applied.
limitations: Application lag is modelled by not advancing raftLog.applied on the transferee; the receipt therefore shows the protocol's behavior given that lag, not how a real application creates it.
The abort was produced by ticking the leader through its own electionTimeout, so the bound observed is in protocol ticks under this harness's scheduling rather than wall-clock time.

The transfer completes in the receipt through the network's MsgTimeoutNow delivery on the retry; no independent completion path (for example a transfer while the leader is also being removed) was exercised.

interpretations.rationale: Index 16 reports the sweep's only output: 60 seeds times 60 steps produced 459 elections and 446 proposals with violations=0, and the event carries the note that absence of violations is a holds-only result for this event set rather than a safety proof. For the four invariants actually checked after every event - at most one leader per term, no index already known committed ever observed with a different term, per-node committed-index monotonicity, and applied <= committed - the receipt therefore contains no counterexample, which is consistent with the source-level explanation that commitment and leadership require quorum-intersecting support under the simple configuration used here (MajorityConfig.CommittedIndex/VoteResult with the joint min/majority semantics). The absence is nevertheless bounded by what the harness actually did: it emitted no violation event of any of the four kinds, and it also emitted no configuration-change or restart event, because the executed case omits both while the registered discriminator named them. I am recording that as a necessary gap and keeping the conclusion scoped to the exercised event set; the defect claim is refuted only in the narrow sense that this event set produced no witness for the suspicion, not because the invariants were established for the protocol.
counterevidence: The sweep's coverage is smaller than the discriminator promised: no ConfChange/ConfChangeV2 proposal, no joint or learner configuration and no restart from persisted storage appeared in the event stream, so the mechanism most likely to threaten the invariants (support counted under a configuration that changes while entries are unapplied) was not part of this receipt.

A zero-violation count over 60 seeds cannot bound the violation rate; it states only that no witness appeared in this fixed event set, and the harness checked committed terms only for indices the nodes actually reported as committed, so an entry committed by a majority but never observed at any checked node is invisible to it.
limitations: Invariant checking happens after each event, not during message delivery, so an intermediate inconsistency that is repaired before the next check point would not be observed.
The committed-entry check compares terms at an index rather than full entry identity, which is adequate for log-matching violations but does not by itself detect a same-term payload difference.
Application is modelled with nextEnts on every step, so the applied index is never more than one event behind committed; a real application's lag patterns are not represented.
No comparison or requirement anchors were declared for this case in the experiment request, so the receipt carries parsed events only and its meaning rests on this interpretation.
